title: How a hash table finds a key
chapters: Seven fruits go into eight buckets
Looking up a key that is not there
notes: The table is an example: seven fruits with stock counts. The bucket each fruit sits in is real, computed with FNV-1a by values.py.
Follow one key all the way. Bytes, then one 32-bit number, then a remainder, then a short walk. Every number on screen is computed, not typed in.
A miss costs the same walk as a hit in the same bucket. The lookup can only say no after the whole bucket.
This is the point to land. The cost is the length of one bucket, which stays short while the table keeps enough buckets.
Each margin number is the click that showed that line. Readers can jump back with the link page.html#N.

clicks.change: Eight empty buckets appear, numbered 0 to 7
clicks.caption: A hash table with eight buckets, numbered 0 to 7, all empty.

clicks.change: Seven fruits drop into their buckets, mango and fig into bucket 5
clicks.caption: Each fruit is stored in bucket number hash(fruit) % 8.

clicks.change: The key fig appears at the top left
clicks.caption: Look up `fig` to get its stock count.

clicks.change: The key's three bytes appear below it, 66 69 67
clicks.caption: The hash function reads bytes, and `fig` in UTF-8 is three bytes.

clicks.change: The 32-bit hash appears below the bytes, 0xc1e49a15
clicks.caption: FNV-1a hashes the three bytes into one 32-bit number.

clicks.change: The remainder after dividing by 8 appears, 5
clicks.caption: The bucket number is the hash modulo 8, the number of buckets.

clicks.change: The remainder glides across to bucket 5
Every bucket but 5 fades
clicks.caption: `fig` can only be in bucket 5, so the others are skipped.

clicks.change: A cross appears beside mango, the first entry in bucket 5
clicks.caption: The first key in bucket 5 is `mango`, not `fig`.

clicks.change: A tick appears beside fig, the second entry
Fig's count, 4, glides out of the table into the empty slot at the left
clicks.caption: `fig` matches, so the lookup returns the count stored with it.

clicks.change: The key pear appears at the top left
clicks.caption: Now look up `pear`, a key that was never stored.

clicks.change: Pear's 32-bit hash appears, 0xd01fc26d
clicks.caption: FNV-1a hashes `pear` the same way, to a different number.

clicks.change: Pear's remainder, 5, comes out under its hash and glides to bucket 5
clicks.caption: That number modulo 8 is also 5, the same bucket as `fig`.

clicks.change: Every bucket but 5 fades
A cross appears beside mango
clicks.caption: `mango` is not `pear`.

clicks.change: A cross appears beside fig
clicks.caption: `fig` is not `pear`.

clicks.change: The end of the list appears after fig
clicks.caption: Bucket 5 has no more keys, so `pear` is not stored.

clicks.change: Every bucket but 5 fades
clicks.caption: Both lookups searched bucket 5 and no other bucket.

clicks.change: The count of comparisons appears at the end of bucket 5, 2 of 7 keys
clicks.caption: A lookup's cost is the number of keys in one bucket.

clicks.change: The lookup function appears, its code dim and the click badges in its margin bright
clicks.caption: Each margin number is the click that showed that step.

clicks.change: The four lines that pick the bucket light
clicks.caption: These lines compute the FNV-1a hash and pick the bucket.

clicks.change: The loop over the bucket lights
clicks.caption: This loop compares `key` with each key in the bucket.

clicks.change: The last line, return None, lights
clicks.caption: If no key matches, the loop ends and the function returns None.
